extracted.intended_audience: educated general readership interested in science, philosophy, and public attitudes toward scientific practice
extracted.subtask_description: An essay discussing causes of public dread and dislike of science, the nature and method of science, contrasts with theology, and the justification for applying scientific method across domains. It analyzes misconceptions, social reactions, and the moral reasoning surrounding scientific practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Science as Systematized Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is simply knowledge classified, systematized, made orderly, impersonal, and exact; as Comte calls it, 'common-sense methodized and extended.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between unmethodized personal experience and science as the organized, communicable experience of many minds condensed into simple laws. Notes there is plenty of knowledge that is not exact and of exact knowledge not methodized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as Method and Doctrine (Twofold Meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science means, first, a general Method, or Logic of Search, applicable to all departments of knowledge; and, secondly, a doctrine or body of truths and hypotheses embracing the results of search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that particular sciences (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, psychology, etc.) are special applications of the general method; although interdependent, each is restricted to its own class of facts and none can legislate for the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational vs Irrational Opposition to Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition to science is rational when protesting against the misplaced application of results from one domain to another; it is irrational when protesting against the rigorous application of scientific logic to inquiries generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the example that objecting to applying mechanical principles to moral questions is rational, whereas rejecting the general logic of systematic inquiry is irrational and obstructs civilization's advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science Demands Exactness (Criterion of Evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science demands exactness and testing by evidence; this insistence on measurement and verifiable observation is central to scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the cook who refuses to measure, and by social reactions that label seekers of evidence as 'bores' or 'narrow'. Emphasizes preferring observation over guessing and weighing evidence rather than accepting wide conclusions without appreciating their data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science's Faith: Verification and Modifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: The faith of Science consists in reliance on principles sought and found by competent inquirers, tested incessantly, open to verification, and modifiable according to new experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with theological faith based on tradition and unverifiable revelation. Examples: trusting the law of gravitation or measured velocity of light by relying on those competent to verify them; faith grounded in conformity with experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological Faith vs Scientific Faith (Credentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological faith relies on statements handed down by tradition of presumed divine origin and not open to empirical verification; scientific faith relies on tested, verifiable, and revisable principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes theological credentials are appealed from sacred texts or moral consciousness; scientific credentials are conformity with experience and repeated testing. Points out variation among traditions and the inability of tradition to supply the same kind of verification as science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Domain Boundaries for Scientific Conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions reached in one department of inquiry should not be allowed to dictate conclusions in another; scientists should not legislate for domains outside their specialized class of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why artists and moralists resist scientific overreach—accepting a chemist's facts but refusing his theories about art—and why misplaced application excuses rational protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Scientific Method to Moral and Social Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of scientific method are to be followed in the moral and social sciences despite greater complication; there is no need for a different 'Logic of Search.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that history, language, religion, psychology, and sociology can be systematized by the same method used in physical sciences; complexity does not warrant introducing another logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as a Social Benefit (Justifying Harm for Knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific work can be justified as a social benefit when it enlarges knowledge and human power; failure to recognize this leads to inconsistent moral judgments about suffering inflicted for different ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts public tolerance of large-scale suffering for commercial or pleasure ends with fury at comparatively small suffering for scientific ends (e.g., vivisection), arguing that if science were recognized as a social benefit, such contradictions would not stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for Criticizing Specific Practices (e.g., Vivisection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of practices like vivisection depends not merely on suffering inflicted but on whether the activity serves verifiable social benefits (advancing remedial agents and scientific truths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes public outrage focuses on scientific purpose rather than amount of suffering; challenges readers to consider motives and social utility consistently across kinds of suffering (sport, industry, experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance Rooted in Native Tendencies and Abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dislike of science partly stems from its abstract, impersonal, and systematic character, which conflicts with humans' concrete, personal experiences and native indolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains need for training and sustaining motives (e.g., appreciation of trigonometry's extended power) to develop interest in remote relations and prolonged observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural vs Natural Explanations and the Two Logics Thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of two Logics (natural and supernatural) underlies the conflict between Science and Theology; invoking supernatural causes for unexplained phenomena persists where natural causes escape immediate penetration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that as natural explanations expand, the domain for supernatural explanations contracts; invoking the supernatural where experience can in principle supply explanations is criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Theological Explanations in Practical Matters (Disease Example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In matters like disease, science seeks causes in known properties of organisms and seeks treatments accordingly, whereas theology invokes supernatural causes (e.g., punishment), which is inconsistent with observation and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out the practical shift from prayer/incantation to drugs/diet even among those who profess supernatural theories; uses disease to illustrate conflict between theological precepts and moral practices informed by science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning Authority of Sacred Texts Where They Conflict with Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: If sacred books make statements at variance with verifiable facts (astronomical, geological, biological), their authority on matters beyond verification is doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that when sacred texts are erroneous on verifiable points, one cannot reasonably accept their unverifiable doctrines; contrasts literal acceptance with interpretive approaches that lead toward rationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism Toward Elevating Innate or Unexplained Phenomena to Higher Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a superstition that regards whatever is innate or unexplained as of higher authority than acquired, empirically verified knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues civilization aims to correct instincts; questions why moral theories of earlier cultures or religious traditions should be considered superior to modern scientific theories; uses music and moral theory examples.
